content: The second part of the Implementation Manual focuses on the technical contributions and standards for prosthetics and orthotics, as outlined by the World Health Organization (WHO). This manual, published in 2017, provides detailed guidance for Member States to improve access to high-quality, affordable prosthetics and orthotics services. It complements the standards presented in Part 1 by offering specific instructions on the what, why, how, who, and when of implementing these standards. The manual aims to assist Member States in analyzing the current state of prosthetics and orthotics services in their countries, setting priorities for implementation, and planning, managing, and improving these services to meet the proposed standards. The manual is structured around four core areas of prosthetics and orthotics services: policy (governance, financing, and information), products (prostheses and orthoses), personnel (workforce), and service provision. While the sections are interconnected, each can be read independently for specific information. The manual also includes country examples to illustrate various topics. The manual emphasizes that it is not a blueprint for service implementation in all countries, as plans and priorities vary depending on local contexts and available resources. Instead, it serves as a framework to stimulate discussion and guide the development of policies, strategic plans, and benchmarks for prosthetics and orthotics services. The manual highlights the importance of involving various stakeholders, including users, families, caregivers, user groups, disabled people's organizations, governments, civil society organizations, service providers, training institutions, professional associations, manufacturers, suppliers, international organizations, and funding agencies. Each stakeholder plays a critical role in establishing, strengthening, and maintaining effective prosthetics and orthotics services. For example, service users and their families should be central to planning, implementing, monitoring, and evaluating services. User groups and disabled people's organizations can represent users' interests, raise awareness, and assist in identifying and referring potential users. Governments are responsible for enacting legislation, formulating policies, and creating national plans to promote the availability and affordability of high-quality assistive devices, including prosthetics and orthotics. Civil society organizations can help raise awareness and increase service uptake among diverse populations. Service providers, whether public, private, or non-governmental, are responsible for delivering services and collecting data for national planning. Professional associations provide collective expertise for planning and promoting services, while manufacturers and suppliers develop and provide cost-effective, high-quality components and materials. Governments are also tasked with establishing a guiding framework for prosthetics and orthotics services, including national laws, policies, plans, standards, and regulations. National plans should set detailed goals and steps for establishing and managing services, while standards should define working methods, processes, practices, infrastructure, and equipment. Governments should regulate training, service provision, products, and the importation and distribution of components and materials. These regulations should be integrated into the national healthcare regulatory system and developed in collaboration with relevant stakeholders.
